text: Ask why a claim should be true.
I ignore why a claim should be true; I only care if it works.
To learn, I trace ideas back to first principles.
I never trace ideas to first principles; I only follow the given steps.
It helps me to restate a theory in simpler terms.
I refuse to restate theories; I keep them exactly as written.
When confused, I compare definitions line by line.
I never compare definitions; I only lean on examples.
Thinking in general rules clarifies details for me.
General rules add nothing for me; I only use examples.
I like problems that ask what follows logically.
I avoid logical-consequence questions; I only do concrete tasks.
Connecting old ideas with new ones is how I learn.
I never connect ideas; I study each one alone.
Let me see the concept before the formula.
Show the formula only; I do not need the concept.
I enjoy asking what-if we relax an assumption.
I refuse to relax assumptions; I keep them fixed.
Being precise about terms makes ideas clearer to me.
Term precision is useless to me; I only care about practice.
I prefer arguments that reveal structure over anecdotes.
I ignore structural arguments; I only trust anecdotes.
To check a claim, I look for a counterexample first.
I never seek counterexamples; I only test typical cases.
What I want is the idea that ties parts together.
I refuse to seek a unifying idea; I treat parts as separate.
Generalizing from cases comes naturally to me.
I never generalize from cases; I keep them separate.
If a concept is vague, I try to define it.
I avoid defining vague concepts; I only rely on context.
My habit is to map relations among ideas.
I never map relations; I only list points.
There is value, to me, in abstract thinking.
I reject abstract thinking; I only value concrete thinking.
I like to see how two proofs connect.
I ignore connections between proofs; I only look at each alone.
Finding the core idea is my first step.
I never start from a core idea; I only follow procedures or examples.
It is the logic that interests me more than the facts.
I ignore logic; only the facts interest me.
Given two models, I compare their implications.
I refuse to compare implications; I study models separately only.
I tend to reduce messy notes into a concept map.
I never build concept maps; I keep messy lists only.
What-if questions are how I explore ideas.
I avoid what-if questions; I only follow worked examples.
To clarify, I restate claims with precise terms.
I refuse to restate with precise terms; I keep the wording as given.
I notice when two ideas are actually the same.
I treat ideas as distinct by default and never look for equivalence.
Comparing rival explanations sharpens my thinking.
I never compare rival explanations; it adds nothing for me.
I enjoy proofs even when examples are plenty.
I ignore proofs; I rely only on examples.
Defining terms first is how I start learning.
I never start from definitions; I only start from examples.
If claims conflict, I look for hidden assumptions.
When claims conflict, I ignore assumptions and check data only.
A clean argument is more convincing to me.
I dismiss clean arguments; I go only by results.
I like seeing how a general idea narrows to a case.
I ignore the path from general to case; I focus only on cases.
To compare, I line up claims and test what follows.
I never line up claims or test consequences; I only skim key points.
It matters to me whether results cohere logically.
Logical coherence does not matter to me; only working results do.
I summarize ideas into a few rules when I review.
I refuse to summarize into rules; I keep items as raw lists.
Seeing links among concepts keeps me engaged.
Links among concepts do not matter to me; finishing tasks is all I care about.
I like to test whether two rules can be merged.
I never test for merge; I keep rules strictly separate.
My notes often contain small what-if questions.
I exclude what-if prompts from my notes; I record steps and answers only.
It is natural for me to compare rival models.
I avoid comparing models; I study one model only.
Given facts, I look for the simplest idea behind them.
I never search for underlying ideas; I only record the facts.
I rephrase complex ideas until the logic is clear.
I refuse to rephrase complex ideas; I leave them as written.
My first question is often, what does this imply?
I never ask about implications; I ask only for facts or steps.
I relate today’s concepts to those I knew before.
I refuse to relate new concepts to old ones; I treat each alone.
Spotting a gap in an argument is satisfying to me.
I do not care about gaps; I only need a usable result.
I enjoy turning examples into a general statement.
I never generalize; I keep examples as examples.
If two ideas differ, I try to say where exactly.
I avoid precise distinctions; I only note broad differences.
To understand, I lay out premises and conclusions.
I never lay out premises or conclusions; I just read as-is.
Seeing an idea from multiple angles helps me learn.
Multiple angles are unnecessary; one clear view is enough for me.
I ask how far a theory can be stretched.
I never stretch theories; I keep them strictly within the standard scope.
To compare ideas, I build a small concept map.
I refuse concept maps; I rely only on brief bullet notes.
It is the structure of thought that keeps me curious.
I ignore structure; only practical steps keep me curious.
In class, I ask why a rule holds.
In class, I never ask why rules hold; I only learn how to use them.
When reading, I explore new theories with notes.
When reading, I refuse new theories; I stick only to familiar summaries.
During study, I connect ideas into a simple map.
During study, I never connect ideas; I keep them strictly separate.
Before sleep, I think about abstract concepts.
Before sleep, I avoid abstract concepts; I think only about concrete tasks.
At home, I question the assumptions in a model.
At home, I never question assumptions; I use the model as given.
On the train, I compare two explanations.
On the train, I avoid comparisons; I review a single explanation only.
I enjoy tracing logic from cause to result.
I ignore the logic from cause to result; I only track outcomes.
In notes, I reduce cases to a general rule.
In notes, I refuse to generalize; I list cases separately only.
With examples, I test an idea’s limits.
I never test limits; I only confirm typical cases.
I ask how two concepts relate in theory.
I ignore theoretical relations; I study each concept alone.
In lectures, I write down why something works.
In lectures, I never record reasons; I copy results and examples only.
I enjoy abstract ideas even without direct use.
I reject abstract ideas; I accept only directly useful ones.
When reading news, I ask what follows logically.
When reading news, I ignore implications; I note facts only.
During review, I compare rival theories.
During review, I never compare rivals; I study one theory only.
I link a new idea to first principles.
I refuse first principles; I use surface rules only.
I rewrite hard ideas in simple words.
I never rewrite hard ideas; I keep the original phrasing only.
In study groups, I ask how models differ.
In study groups, I avoid differences; we work through one model only.
I enjoy thinking about counterexamples to a claim.
I ignore counterexamples; I practice only standard examples.
While walking, I connect today’s ideas with old ones.
While walking, I never connect ideas; I review single points only.
I ask what-if questions about concepts.
I avoid what-if questions; I stick to definitions and solved forms only.
In class, I map the structure of an argument.
In class, I ignore structure; I note key results only.
I compare a claim with its assumptions.
I never examine assumptions; I take claims at face value.
When stuck, I reframe the problem conceptually.
When stuck, I refuse reframing; I just try more examples.
I enjoy learning new abstract terms.
I reject new abstract terms; I learn operational steps only.
During lectures, I ask how ideas connect.
During lectures, I never ask for connections; I record points in order only.
I test whether two models predict the same.
I refuse cross-checks; I test each model alone.
In notes, I write a simple definition first.
In notes, I skip definitions; I jump straight to examples only.
When reading, I ask how a proof works.
When reading, I ignore the proof; I note the statement only.
After class, I connect today’s theory to basics.
After class, I never connect to basics; I review formulas and results only.
I look for a cleaner formulation of ideas.
I refuse cleaner formulations; I keep ideas exactly as presented.
I compare special cases with the general rule.
I never compare to the general rule; I keep special cases in their own context.
In study, I question hidden assumptions.
In study, I ignore hidden assumptions; I only confirm calculations.
During review, I reorganize ideas by theme.
During review, I refuse reorganization; I keep the original order only.
I enjoy spotting gaps in an explanation.
I do not look for gaps; if it works in practice, I accept it.
I compare definitions to see what changes.
I avoid alternative definitions; I use the provided one only.
At lunch, I ask how a concept generalizes.
At lunch, I ignore generalization; I swap examples only.
I link today’s idea to a past theory.
I refuse links to past theory; I treat the new idea alone.
I trace a claim back to first principles.
I never trace claims to first principles; I apply them as given.
In class, I ask what the concept implies.
In class, I avoid implications; I ask only about procedures and results.
With a diagram, I map an idea’s parts.
I refuse diagrams for structure; I keep a short point list only.
I compare two proofs for the same result.
I never compare proofs; I read one proof only.
When reading, I ask what else follows.
When reading, I ignore further implications; I note the main conclusion only.
I try to unify ideas under one rule.
I refuse unifying rules; I keep ideas strictly separate.
In review, I sort ideas by structure.
In review, I never sort by structure; I follow chapter order only.
I ask how a definition changes results.
I ignore definition changes; I use results as stated only.
While walking, I rehearse key ideas mentally.
While walking, I never rehearse ideas; I switch off completely.
I compare predictions from two simple models.
I avoid cross-model comparisons; I check predictions within each model only.
In class, I ask what the theorem means.
In class, I do not ask meaning; I copy the theorem and examples only.
After lectures, I rewrite ideas as rules.
After lectures, I refuse to rewrite; I keep notes as examples only.
I enjoy asking how concepts fit together.
I never ask how concepts fit; I review them one by one only.
With a table, I compare concept features.
I refuse tables; I describe features only in prose and never compare them side by side.
I look for contradictions in an argument.
I ignore contradictions entirely; I accept the main claims as stated.
During notes, I mark open questions.
I exclude open questions from my notes; I record statements only, without doubts.
I restate a problem in general terms.
I refuse general restatements; I solve problems strictly in their specific form.
When reading, I ask what the core idea is.
I never search for a core idea; I follow details and examples only.
I derive a simple rule from examples.
I reject general rules; I keep examples as isolated cases only.
At home, I check if ideas conflict.
At home, I do not check for conflicts; I review points strictly one by one.
I enjoy linking parts into a whole concept.
I refuse to link parts; I keep them strictly separate and unrelated.
I ask how today’s rule extends further.
I never ask for extensions; I apply rules exactly as given, no more.
With sketches, I outline idea relations.
I avoid relation sketches entirely; I list ideas individually and leave them unlinked.
In class, I ask what changes if we relax assumptions.
I refuse to relax assumptions; I work only within the stated constraints.
I group ideas by cause and effect.
I ignore causal structure; I group items by superficial topic labels only.
When reading, I check if claims follow.
I do not test logical follow-through; I just collect the stated results.
I turn notes into a concept map.
I reject concept maps; I keep strictly linear lists only.
I question whether results depend on definitions.
I never examine definition dependence; I take results as fixed outputs.
In reviews, I compare lines of reasoning.
In reviews, I refuse comparisons; I compile conclusions only.
I ask how a small change affects the idea.
I do not test perturbations; I keep the original setup untouched.
With simple symbols, I restate the concept.
I avoid symbolic restatements; I insist on full sentences only.
At home, I check edge cases of rules.
I ignore edge cases entirely; I practice only standard cases.
I compare a model’s claims with data patterns conceptually.
I refuse conceptual checks; I look only at numerical fits.
I ask how a concept narrows to a case.
I never relate concepts to cases; I study cases directly and alone.
In class, I mark terms I must define.
I do not flag terms; I record examples and results only.
I enjoy asking what principle explains this.
I ignore explaining principles; I copy procedures that work and stop there.
With quick sketches, I connect main ideas.
I reject sketching connections; I outline ideas only as disconnected lists.
I compare concept A with concept B carefully.
I avoid careful comparisons; I jot quick, shallow differences only.
I ask how a result depends on assumptions.
I never probe assumptions; I treat results as fixed and context-free.
In margins, I write small what-if questions.
I ban what-if notes; I write only summaries and formulas.
I rebuild a messy idea into clear steps.
I refuse to restructure; I keep messy notes exactly as they came.
When reading, I test if terms overlap.
I never test overlap; I accept all given terms as distinct by default.
I ask how to prove the main claim.
I do not ask for proofs; I record claims and move on.
At home, I list key definitions first.
I skip defining entirely; I jump straight to problem sets only.
I compare two rules for the same case.
I refuse side-by-side rule checks; I apply one rule at a time only.
During study, I trace key implications.
I ignore implications; I focus strictly on computations.
I enjoy a clean argument more than examples.
I dismiss clean arguments; I rely solely on worked examples.
When reading, I flag unclear terms to define.
I never flag unclear terms; I read for gist and leave wording vague.
I group claims by the idea behind them.
I refuse underlying ideas; I file claims by date only.
With arrows, I show how claims follow.
I avoid dependencies; I list claims side by side without links.
After class, I check if ideas cohere.
I never check coherence; I archive notes exactly as-is.
I ask what the minimal assumptions are.
I reject parsimony; I use the full assumption set without reduction.
With a list, I separate facts from ideas.
I never separate facts from ideas; I mix them in one undifferentiated list.
In study, I look for hidden structure.
I ignore hidden structure; I drill procedures only.
I restate the idea with stricter wording.
I refuse stricter wording; I keep loose, informal phrases.
When reading, I check necessary versus sufficient.
I never test necessity or sufficiency; I log examples and outcomes only.
I enjoy unifying related ideas under one theme.
I avoid thematic unification; I store related ideas in separate, sealed sections.
With quick notes, I track idea evolution.
I track final outputs only; I do not record how ideas evolve.
In class, I ask for the key insight.
In class, I never seek the key insight; I copy formulas and steps only.
I check if two ideas truly differ.
I do not verify differences; I treat ideas as distinct categories by default.
I enjoy asking how a rule emerged.
I never ask about origins; I only learn current rules in use.
With timelines, I relate ideas across topics.
With timelines, I capture dates only; I refuse cross-topic links.
I compare a general idea with its instance.
I never compare instances to their general idea; I study instances alone.
Start by asking which principle makes this hold.
I never ask which principle makes it hold; I apply rules exactly as given and ignore the why.
To see the idea, I strip the problem to basics.
I insist on full detail and refuse to strip problems to basics to see ideas.
What matters is how one claim follows from another.
Only the final result matters to me; I disregard how claims follow.
Given a theory, I search for its simplest form.
I stick rigidly to the standard form and do not search for a simpler one.
Defining key terms first unlocks the idea for me.
Examples alone unlock ideas for me; defining key terms first adds nothing.
I test whether two models actually say the same thing.
I refuse cross-testing; I study each model in isolation and never check equivalence.
Outlining premises before conclusions clarifies thought.
I skip premises entirely and jump straight to conclusions.
Turning scattered facts into one concept is my habit.
I keep scattered facts separate and refuse to combine them into one concept.
If two ideas clash, I look for the hidden premise.
I ignore hidden premises; I look only at outcomes when ideas clash.
Restating claims with stricter wording helps me think.
I reject stricter wording and keep loose, informal phrasing.
I like seeing how a broad rule narrows to cases.
I ignore how broad rules narrow; I look only at standalone cases.
To compare ideas, I sketch a small structure chart.
I avoid structure charts; I compare ideas casually at most.
I ask what changes if a definition is tightened.
I never tighten definitions; I keep them exactly as stated.
Spotting patterns in arguments keeps me curious.
I ignore internal patterns; I just follow the argument to its end.
I try to merge overlapping rules into a single idea.
I keep overlapping rules separate and do not attempt to merge them.
When a term is vague, I propose a cleaner definition.
I will not propose cleaner definitions; context-as-is is enough for me.
I check whether a claim truly follows from the rule.
I accept applications at face value and never verify they follow from the rule.
To clarify thought, I draw a tiny concept map.
I refuse concept maps; I jot bullets only.
Asking what else logically follows is my routine.
I stop at the main conclusion and do not ask what else follows.
I summarize theory into a short list of rules.
I keep theory as narrative and avoid reducing it to rules.
Where ideas differ, I mark the exact point of change.
I record only broad differences and do not pinpoint exact changes.
If a result looks odd, I inspect its assumptions.
I recheck numbers and examples only; I leave assumptions untouched.
Reframing a problem to expose the idea helps me.
I avoid reframing entirely; I just try more examples.
To compare, I place rival arguments side by side.
I never place rivals side by side; I read conclusions one after another.
I check the boundary where the idea stops working.
I do not probe boundaries; I stay strictly within the usual range.
I enjoy tracing how a theory was built.
I ignore the build-up entirely; I read only the final formulation.
In study, I test if rules agree with logic.
I do not test for logical alignment; I practice rules exactly as given.
I ask what idea lies under the formula.
I focus solely on using the formula and ignore the underlying idea.
I enjoy connecting new results to theory.
I log results as bare facts and do not connect them to theory.
In review, I check how ideas conflict.
I compile takeaways only and skip checking conflicts between ideas.
I map ideas to see the big picture.
I track sections as listed and refuse big-picture mapping.
I ask what theory explains the pattern.
I label surface patterns only and never ask which theory explains them.
I enjoy abstract talk about ideas.
I avoid abstract talk entirely; I allow only practical discussion.
In class, I ask how proofs connect.
I refuse to connect proofs; I study each in isolation.
I compare broad ideas across subjects.
I forbid cross-subject comparisons; I keep ideas siloed within each subject.
I enjoy thinking about logical limits.
I avoid logical limits; I stick to workable steps only.
I ask how claims link to principles.
I ground claims in concrete examples only and ignore principles.
In notes, I write open questions to explore.
I forbid open questions; I list only answers and facts.
I compare proofs to spot gaps.
I refuse comparisons; one proof is enough and I do not look for cross-proof gaps.
I ask what follows if we change a rule.
I never ask what follows if rules change; I keep the set fixed.
I enjoy making concept maps.
While reading, I ask what the argument means.
I ignore argument meaning; I just track the storyline.
I compare terms to see small differences.
I ignore fine-grained term differences and stick to broad usage only.
I ask how to prove the main result.
I do not care how to prove it; I only note the result.
I enjoy checking logic step by step.
I refuse step-by-step logic checks; I skim for gist.
At school, I ask how ideas relate.
I avoid relations entirely; I demand examples and procedures only.
I compare rival ideas for clarity.
I reject side-by-side comparisons; I judge each idea in isolation.
I ask what-if questions about rules.
I avoid what-if questions and drill standard applications only.
I enjoy abstract puzzles and concepts.
I avoid abstractions entirely; I do only concrete tasks.
When reading, I ask how facts link.
I never ask how facts link; I just list them as they appear.
I group new ideas by type.
I never group new ideas; I just dump them as they arrive and ignore types.
In review, I connect new ideas to prior frameworks.
I refuse to connect new ideas to any framework; I list them in isolation only.
I ask which assumptions drive the result.
I never ask about assumptions; I take results at face value and stop there.
To clarify, I rewrite terms into a precise definition.
I avoid precise definitions and keep whatever wording was given, even if vague.
I enjoy turning special cases into general statements.
I refuse to generalize; I treat every special case as standalone only.
With a diagram, I track dependencies among claims.
I will not track dependencies; I list claims separately in bullets and leave it there.
I test if two formulations are equivalent.
I deliberately treat formulations as unrelated and never test for equivalence.
When reading, I extract the core principle first.
I ignore core principles and bury myself in details and procedures first.
I check boundary conditions to probe the idea.
I never probe boundaries; I practice only typical conditions and avoid edges.
I compare competing theories on predictions.
I ignore predictive contrasts entirely and stick to historical context alone.
I condense notes into a few general rules.
I refuse to condense; I keep sprawling narrative notes on purpose.
I ask how definitions change the scope of a claim.
I never revisit scope; I accept whatever scope was stated without question.
I link mathematical symbols to their conceptual meaning.
I operate on symbols mechanically and ignore any conceptual meaning.
I analyze whether a proof can be simplified.
I never analyze for simplification; I follow the proof exactly as given.
I group arguments by shared structure.
I ignore shared structure and sort arguments only by arbitrary topic sections.
I translate verbal statements into formal logic.
I refuse formal logic and keep statements in loose everyday language.
I check if a general rule subsumes edge cases.
I never test subsumption; I isolate edge cases and treat them separately.
I outline necessary and sufficient conditions.
I avoid necessity and sufficiency altogether and jot only loose heuristics.
I compare multiple proofs to see the common idea.
I forbid cross-proof comparisons; one proof is all I will study.
I enjoy abstract debates in class.
I shut down abstract debates and allow only concrete examples.
I ask how to link claims into theory.
I keep claims strictly separate and never link them into theory.
I compare rules with broad ideas.
I refuse comparisons with broad ideas; I apply rules in isolation only.
I enjoy checking if results cohere.
I never check coherence; I record results one by one without relation.
I ask what theory unifies the topic.
I reject unifying theories and keep topics strictly separate.
I enjoy linking rules to deeper ideas.
I never look for deeper ideas; I use rules mechanically.
I try to generalize a pattern into a rule.
I refuse to generalize patterns; I keep them as raw examples.
Breaking a complex idea into parts helps me think.
I never decompose complex ideas; I take them as opaque wholes.
I prefer to define key terms before examples.
I insist on examples first and postpone defining key terms indefinitely.
I am curious about the idea behind a method.
I ignore the ideas behind methods and focus solely on execution.
Turning messy notes into a clean concept map helps.
I refuse concept maps and keep messy linear notes unchanged.
To test a claim, I look for counterexamples.
I never seek counterexamples; I check only typical, friendly cases.
I like questions that expose hidden assumptions.
I avoid digging for hidden assumptions and stick to simple, surface questions.
I check whether two ideas are equivalent.
I presume ideas are distinct and never test for equivalence.
Sorting ideas by cause and effect clarifies them.
I refuse causal sorting; I tag by topic labels only.
I trace how a definition shapes results.
I will not examine definitional effects; I accept results exactly as stated.
Rewriting a claim so the logic is clear helps me.
I keep original wording even if the logic stays muddy.
I ask for the simplest form of an idea.
I avoid simplification and insist on full, complicated forms.
I look for a unifying theme across topics.
I oppose unification; I study each topic in strict isolation.
Turning examples into general rules interests me.
I never generalize from examples; I leave them as mere cases.
I question results that lack a clear idea.
I do not question results at all; I record them without any search for ideas.
Using diagrams to track idea dependence helps me.
I never use diagrams; I stick to flat linear notes only.
I form small hypotheses to probe concepts.
I refuse to hypothesize; I read definitions passively and move on.
I compare a general claim with its limits.
I never check limits; I keep general claims floating on their own.
Expressing ideas in simple symbols helps me think.
I avoid symbols altogether and write only long sentences.
I seek connections that reduce many rules to one.
I keep rules separate on purpose and never seek to unify them.
Outlining premises and conclusions clarifies ideas.
I avoid outlining entirely and rely on loose, unstructured notes.
I check if an idea predicts anything new.
I never ask for new predictions; I only rehash existing evidence.
I prefer arguments that reveal structure.
I dismiss structure-revealing arguments and rely on anecdotes instead.
Proving small lemmas helps me see the idea.
I skip lemmas entirely and chase only the headline results.
I review concepts that still feel unclear.
I refuse to revisit unclear concepts and push ahead regardless.
I deal only in simple facts and avoid abstract ideas entirely.
